svg.title: Changing a DNS record with caches in mind
svg.desc: A timeline for migrating a record. Before the change, by at least the old TTL plus a margin, lower the record's TTL, for example from 3600 to 60. At time T, change the record and keep the old endpoint serving. At T plus the new TTL most clients have moved: verify from several resolvers and watch the old endpoint drain. Later, raise the TTL again. Mistake to avoid: changing the address and lowering the TTL at the same time. Also remember that resolvers may clamp TTLs or serve stale data, a JVM caches independently, and low TTLs cost queries without guaranteeing speed.
svg.text: Migration with caches in mind
T − (old TTL + margin)
Lower the record's TTL (say 3600 → 60). Caches holding the old record
keep the OLD TTL until it expires, so wait at least the old TTL before
relying on the new one.
T
Change the record. Keep the old endpoint serving: some caches, long-lived
connections and misbehaving clients will still use it.
T + new TTL
Most clients have moved. Verify from several resolvers and networks
(dnslab watch, dig @…), and watch the old endpoint's traffic drain.
Later
Raise the TTL again.
Mistake to avoid
Changing the address and lowering the TTL at the same time: caches already holding the record
ignore the new TTL until theirs expires.
Also remember
Resolvers may clamp TTLs (cache-min-ttl, cache-max-ttl), serve stale data when the authority is
unreachable (RFC 8767), and a JVM caches independently.
Low TTLs cost queries; they do not guarantee speed.
